actionable deceit and bad-faith maneuvering.1 
Context of the 13 Harrison Street Dispute 
The dispute centers on a structurally imbalanced, two-unit condominium located at 13 Harrison 
Street in New York City.1 Arnulf Damerau, via his entity 13 Harrison LLC, controls Unit 2, holding 
a 75% majority interest and roughly 9,000 square feet of developable space.1 Michael and 
Alexis Bleich hold a 25% minority interest in Unit 1, which is significantly smaller and plagued by 
structural violations.1 
Conflict erupted when Damerau initiated a multi-million-dollar structural alteration of Unit 2.1 
The proposed development included a complete gut renovation, a vertical enlargement 
involving the addition of new floors, and a comprehensive reconstruction, or "blowout," of the 
building's main roof area.1 Because the Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) 
equipment servicing Bleich's Unit 1 had been situated on the building's main roof for over 
fifteen years, the planned renovation necessitated the temporary or permanent relocation of 
this equipment.1 
Rather than engaging in good-faith logistical coordination, Bleich and Giacovas engineered a 
"highly sophisticated, weaponized pressure mechanism" designed to paralyze the renovation 
through preliminary injunctions, thereby imposing massive carrying costs on Damerau to force 
an unearned, disproportionate financial buyout.1 
Actionable Deceit and FAR/Roof Rights Misrepresentations 
To secure the extraordinary equitable relief of a preliminary injunction, Robert Giacovas drafted 
and filed verified pleadings containing material, knowing misrepresentations of fact regarding 
property rights.1 
Under New York Judiciary Law § 487, an attorney who engages in intentional deceit directed at 
a court is guilty of a misdemeanor and forfeits treble damages to the injured party.1 Crucially, 
following the Court of Appeals precedent in Bill Birds, Inc. v. Stein Law Firm, establishing liability 
requires proving the attorney made a false statement of fact with scienter, not merely 
advancing a non-meritorious legal argument.1 
In the Verified Complaint (NYSCEF DOC. NO. 2), Giacovas asserted that the Bleichs, by virtue of 
their 25% common interest, held possessory, developmental, and financial rights to the 
building's "main roof area" and the Floor Area Ratio (FAR) required for Unit 2's vertical 
enlargement.1 The pleading categorically alleged that the roof blowout would "permanently 
'destroy Plaintiffs' 25% interest in the Building's roof'".1
